speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Banks, finance companies and insurance companies that are covered under the two schemes are called Scheme Members.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The DI Scheme was introduced in 2006 to provide a basic level of protection to small depositors.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: At that time, the Scheme insured Singapore dollar deposits up to S$20,000 per depositor per full bank or finance company.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In 2011, the insured amount was raised to S$50,000.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Policy Owners’ Protection Scheme was set up in 2011 to protect policy owners for commonly purchased insurance policies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Scheme provides compensation for life, accident and health, compulsory and specified Singapore personal lines insurance policies, such as motor, personal property or travel insurances, in the event that a direct life or general insurer fails.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Both Schemes are supported by Funds established under the DI-PPF Act, which are, in turn, built up through contributions from Scheme Members and investment returns.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Singapore Deposit Insurance Corporation (SDIC) administers both Schemes and the respective Funds.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) conducts regular reviews to ensure that the Schemes continue to provide adequate protection to depositors and policy owners, enhance operation of the Schemes and to take into consideration developments in the Singapore financial market and international practices, standards and guidance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In MAS’ most recent review, it also consulted the industry and other stakeholders on its proposals to enhance the Schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This Bill proposes legislative amendments to give effect to the following changes: one, strengthen the protection for depositors and policy owners; two, facilitate an efficient compensation payout process; and three, align the Schemes more closely with international standards and norms.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: There are two main changes to the DI Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: While there is no international standard on the level of coverage, our objective is to ensure that the vast majority of depositors should be fully covered.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: A survey by the International Association of Deposit Insurers found that the international norm is to fully cover about 90% of all insured depositors.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For example, the US, UK, Hong Kong and Malaysia reported full coverage for over 90% of insured depositors.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: When we raised the limit to S$50,000 in 2011, it fully covered over 90% of insured depositors.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Since then, incomes have grown and savings have also increased.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: As a result, S$50,000 fully covered about 87% of insured depositors today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The second change is to raise the annual premium contributions to the DI Fund.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Currently, every DI Scheme member makes annual premium contributions of two to seven basis points of their insured deposit base to the Fund.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The premium increase of one basis point strikes a balance between a reasonable fund build-up period and the financial costs to the industry.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Bill will introduce a definition for “personal” insurance policies, to be one that is owned by a natural person.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The effect of this amendment is to extend protection to claims on damage to properties owned and used by individuals, even if these properties are sometimes used for commercial purposes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This change addresses a potential protection gap today, given that more individuals are using their personal properties for commercial purposes, such as using their cars to provide private hire transport services.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Bill will also give MAS the flexibility to prescribe, in regulations, caps on compensation payouts for specific classes or types of policy or claim event insured under the Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Currently, there are caps on compensation payout for life insurance, but not for specified Singapore personal lines insurance policies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This means that the fund could potentially be exposed to very large claims which could translate into higher premium rates for all consumers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This amendment will allow MAS to mitigate the exposure of the Scheme to very large claims and contain the potential of rising premium rates.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: First, the Bill will include voluntary winding up as a trigger for compensation payout under both Schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Currently, MAS may make a determination for compensation to be paid out when: one, a Scheme member is wound up by a Court in Singapore or elsewhere; or two, MAS is of the opinion that a Scheme member is insolvent, unable or likely to become unable to meet its obligations or about to suspend payments.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Hence, there is no trigger for payout in the event of a winding up of a Scheme member that is voluntary and not ordered by a Court.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This could potentially result in uncertainty and undue delays in payments to depositors and policy owners.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The amendment closes this gap and expedites the compensation process.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Bill will enhance legal protection for directors, employees, officers and agents working for SDIC, the administrator of the Schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Currently, SDIC officers are provided legal immunity against liability if they carry out their duties in good faith and with reasonable care.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: One of SDIC’s primary objectives is to ensure that compensation is made out to depositors and policy owners as quickly as possible in the event a payout is triggered.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: While we expect SDIC to perform its duties with care, making it a strict legal standard could impair the ability of a deposit insurer to carry out their functions expeditiously in a crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The officers may become overly cautious to ensure that their actions are unquestionably reasonable.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The removal of the requirement for “reasonable care” will bring SDIC in line with DI agencies internationally.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: SDIC officers will still be subjected to the standard of “good faith”.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Fraudulent and malicious acts will continue to be excluded from legal immunity.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Bill will accord SDIC increased budgetary autonomy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The current Act requires SDIC to present annual estimates of its income and expenditure and the Funds to the Minister for approval.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: SDIC will continue to submit to the Minister annual reports of its expenditures and revenues and be accountable for the management of its budget.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Bill has laid out several key amendments to ensure the level of protection for depositors and policy owners remains adequate.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Today, I have a few points to highlight as well as offer some suggestions.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In such situations, family members of the policy holder who has passed on have to see if there are any notices of premium payments or insurance statements to have an idea of which insurance companies to contact.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is getting more difficult with paperless e-statements.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Sometimes, we have also had a situation where the policy holder may not stay with the other family members and statements are sent to the address of the policy holder only.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As such, family members and beneficiaries may not even know of the existence of such insurance policies.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Right now, there is an online register launched by Life Insurance Association Singapore for members of the public to check on unclaimed insurance payouts.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But this is only where the insurance companies already knew that the insured has passed away and the amount has become claimable.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Insurance companies are also not the best party to contact the next-of-kin of the policy holder as, very often, such contact information is not collected or, if collected, is not updated regularly.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I believe there is a similar situation for cash in bank accounts where the account holder has passed on but the family members do not know of the existence of the bank account and so do not approach the bank to submit a claim on the money in the account.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As such, it would be good if a central registry can also keep track of what bank accounts each individual has.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The cost of operating this Central Registry can be recovered by legislating that all monies which are unclaimed despite the best efforts of the Registrar to contact the next of kin will go to the state.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope the relevant authorities can take into account my suggestions that I have made today.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, I will pose some questions relating to the Bill’s provisions and the nature of these two schemes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At this point, I declare my interest as the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of a market research and business consulting firm that works with various commercial and governmental entities in the financial services sector locally and globally.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How prompt would be the compensation to depositors and policy owners?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of course, this would vary on a case-by-case basis, depending on the complexity of each case.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But does SDIC aim for a specific timeframe within which the compensation should be paid, such as, for example, one month, three months or six months?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The longer the process takes, of course, the higher the potential loss of interest income and, hence, the opportunity cost to depositors and policy owners.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the DI Fund, it is stated on the SDIC’s website that “the DI Fund will be invested in safe and liquid assets, such as securities issued by the Singapore Government or MAS, deposits with MAS, any debenture or debt security issued by Singapore Sukuk Pte Ltd, and other assets approved by the Minister.” For the PPF Fund, it is stated that, “The PPF Life Fund and PPF General Fund will be invested in safe and liquid assets, such as securities issued by the Singapore Government or MAS, deposits with MAS, any debenture or debt security issued by Singapore Sukuk Pte Ltd and other assets approved by the Minister.” Does SDIC outsource the management of the Funds to asset management institutions to manage?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And, if so, what is the mandate for these asset management institutions, given that the Minister can approve investment in assets other than Singapore Government instruments?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are there prescribed limits to the kinds of asset classes and asset characteristics that investments can be extended to, for example, weighted fixed income products with a specific high rating from independent credit rating agencies?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, is the ability of the DI and PPF Funds to meet their obligations in respect of the coverage limits regularly reviewed and stress-tested by MAS, or required to be self-reviewed and stress-tested?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In an insolvency case involving a large bank or insurer or a number of these, this ability could be put to the test.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fourthly, on the change whereby the accounts of SDIC need not be audited by the Auditor-General's Office (AGO) or an agency appointed in consultation with the AGO, I would like to ask why the AGO need no longer play a role with respect to the external audit for these Funds?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, lastly, on the website of SDIC, it is stated that MAS may exempt life or general insurers from being members of the PPF scheme.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: May we know how many insurers are so exempted and what measures are in place to protect policy holders in these cases?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a regional financial hub, this also makes us more susceptible to fallouts from any global financial crisis.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the changes in US trade policies and its demand to renegotiate pacts signed by the previous government, which have created bouts of insecurity, anything can happen if the talks do not turn out well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, it is prudent for us to shore up the levees before the storm.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are known to have a strong culture to save our money, and I am aware of people who would open several bank accounts with different banks in order to get their deposits fully covered under the existing scheme.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This enhanced policy will give better protection to those depositors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Also, in an ageing community, some of the savers are retired seniors and the protection would certainly give them much comfort.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On this note, I would like to also emphasise the importance of communicating the coverage of DI to the elderly so that they understand the span of coverage.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My concern is that this additional premium will eventually be passed down to customers down the road.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This may take the form of decreased returns to customers, or higher costs and premiums for financial products and so forth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister if MAS takes an oversight of how the banks impose charges on their products and services as a result of this latest move.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, Mr Deputy Speaker, in a gig economy, many freelancers and self-employed people are using their personal properties for commercial purposes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, in doing so, who bears the additional cost of coverage?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With these amendments, there is a need to step up on educating the public on these various schemes so consumers can make wise choices and benefit from the available policies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Community centres are a good choice for the elderly to be informed about these latest changes as well, in terms of DI, for example.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And as schools start recognising the importance of imparting financial literacy to students, such Government schemes should be shared with students at secondary or tertiary levels.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Agents and providers of financial products should also be more proactive in keeping consumers informed of their rights, in particular, the latest changes in the DI Scheme and their limits.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On behalf of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister-in-charge of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, let me now address their questions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat is concerned that costs of higher premium contributions may be passed on to customers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS had considered the potential cost implications on Scheme Members when proposing these changes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We do not expect the Scheme Members to pass these costs to customers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked who would bear the additional cost for extending the coverage of the Policy Owners’ Protection Scheme to cover the personal properties used for commercial purposes, and if this would result in a rise of premiums.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The current annual contributions paid by the Scheme Members make up less than 0.2% of the total gross premiums written by the general insurance industry for insurance policies covered under the Scheme.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The extension of coverage of the Scheme accounts for a small fraction of the 0.2%.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hence, the increase in contributions paid by the Scheme Members will also not be material.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We do not expect Scheme Members to pass the cost to policy owners.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat also highlighted the importance of educating the public on the coverage of the Schemes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Proper awareness of the coverage of the Schemes will help depositors and policy owners to make informed financial decisions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: SDIC has in place a public education programme already and we will take in Mr Saktiandi Supaat's suggestions in future efforts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: SDIC and MAS will continue to work together to raise awareness of the changes to the Schemes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, he asked how promptly can we expect compensatory payments to be made.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Leon Perera also asked how the DI-PPF Fund monies are managed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Fund's monies are managed by SDIC, the administrator of the Schemes and Funds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The management of the Funds are not outsourced.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The SDIC Board, therefore, oversee the management of the Funds directly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It has established an investment policy for the Funds, covering investment philosophy and objective, permitted investments and markets, authority limits and asset allocation guidelines.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The procedures, internal controls and disclosure and reporting on the investment holdings are audited by a public accounting firm annually and this is in accordance with the requirements of the DI-PPF Act and the Singapore Financial Reporting Standards.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Leon Perera also asked what kind of insurers are exempted from being PPF members.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Actually, all licensed direct life and general insurers are, by default, PPF Scheme Members except for captive insurers and certain insurers that write very specialised risks.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, licensed direct insurers that do not write any of the insurance policies that are covered by the PPF Fund can seek exemption from being PPF Scheme Members.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing suggested that a central repository be set up to assist a deceased's next-of-kin and beneficiaries to find out what life insurance policies and bank accounts the deceased had.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The question is not related to the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Notwithstanding, there is currently a process in place for the next-of-kin to find and claim the assets of a family member who has passed on.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Depending on whether the deceased had made a will, the next-of-kin may apply to the Court for a Grant of Probate or Letters of Administration.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Once the Grant or Letter is issued, the next-of-kin may bring the Grant or Letter to the banks and life insurance companies to find out if there are monies or assets belonging to the deceased.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A central repository could offer the prospect of a convenient one-stop shop.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, a central repository works best if it is provided with up-to-date information and there is universal participation by the financial institutions, depositors and policy owners.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There could be privacy concerns if participation in the repository is made mandatory.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A central repository also does not eliminate the need for the next-of-kin to gather supporting documents to prove their claim to the estate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Nonetheless, Mr Yee Chia Hsing’s proposal highlights the importance of Singaporeans keeping their family and loved ones informed of their financial arrangements.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I just have two questions which I believe had not been addressed yet, unless I missed it.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I just want to know why that change was made.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On stress-testing, because the investment policy is a conservative one, targeted at preservation of principal, therefore, no stress-testing is actually required because we actually require a capital preservation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, on AGO, because SDIC is a company and, therefore, under the Companies Act and in accordance with the Act, it is a public accounting firm that audits it, rather than AGO, which audits Government agencies.
